sections.html:
Decedents' estates are handled under Title 43 of the Code of Alabama. Chapter 2, Administration of Estates, is the main procedural map, and its twenty articles follow the order of a typical estate. These are the ones a house seller meets most:

ArticleWhat it covers
2Grant of letters testamentary or of administration
3Notice of appointment of executors or administrators
4Bonds of executors and administrators
13Collection, inventory and appraisement of personal property
15Claims and debts
17Renting and sale of real estate
18Settlements and distributions
19Insolvent estates
20Probate Procedure Act

If you want to sell an inherited house, article 17 and the Probate Procedure Act in article 20 matter most, since they deal with how real estate can be rented or sold.

sections.h2: Who can sell an inherited house
sections.html:
Authority usually rests with the personal representative the probate court appoints. That person is an executor when a will names one and an administrator when there is no will. A buyer's title company will want to see the appointment before it relies on anyone's signature.

Section 43-2-843 lists what a personal representative may properly do, unless the will or a court order says otherwise. Several items bear on a house sale: holding assets until distribution, performing the decedent's contracts to convey land, paying taxes and other costs of administration, insuring the assets, hiring appraisers and attorneys, and leasing property for a term not over one year.

When the decedent had an enforceable contract to convey land, the representative may deliver a deed for cash, or deliver a deed in escrow so that the proceeds go to the decedent's successors when paid. A buyer's title company will ask to see that paperwork.

sections.h2: Who inherits when there is no will?
sections.html:
Intestacy rules decide the heirs when no valid will exists. Section 43-8-42 sets the order for everything that does not go to a surviving spouse, or for the whole estate if there is no spouse.

  • First to the decedent's issue, equally if they are of the same degree of kinship, or by representation if not.
  • With no issue, to the decedent's parent or parents equally.
  • With no issue or parents, to the issue of the parents or either of them, by representation.
  • If none of those survive, to grandparents and their issue, half to the paternal side and half to the maternal side.

That order is why one inherited house so often has several owners. If children share equally, every child has a stake in the sale, and the personal representative needs a clear route to the buyer.

A house cannot be sold until a person has authority to sign for the estate, and the probate court grants it. Letters, notice of appointment, bonds and the inventory of personal property each get their own article, and any can slow things when records are scattered or relatives disagree. The section also allows a representative to insure estate assets, borrow or advance money to protect the estate, and park idle cash in federally insured interest-bearing accounts.

Claims against the estate come next. Article 15 handles claims and debts, article 19 addresses insolvent estates, and article 18 governs settlements and distributions. A representative who sells the house before sorting out the debts may face questions from heirs or creditors later.

Property taxes keep running meanwhile. They are due October 1 and delinquent after December 31, and paying taxes and assessments incident to administration is on the list of things a personal representative may do.

sections.h2: What the deed costs to record
sections.html:
Section 40-22-1 puts a privilege or license tax on recording: 50 cents per $500 of value, counting any leftover fraction of $500, for instruments conveying property worth over $500. Value covered by a mortgage or vendor's lien that already paid mortgage tax comes off the taxable amount.

  • Attach proof of the real sale price, or the real value if nothing was sold, using the Revenue Department's form.
  • At presentation, the judge of probate calculates the tax.
  • Without proof, the tax follows the latest assessment, and a penalty can be added.
  • Holding back proof on purpose after a request, or supplying false proof, costs $100 or 25 percent of the tax, whichever is higher.

One exemption covers deeds executed for nominal consideration to perfect a title. Before you assume yours qualifies, ask the county probate office how an estate transfer is treated.

Each county's judge of probate doubles as the deed recording office. So one courthouse shows up twice, in the estate matter and in the real estate closing, and the office that opened the estate file is the one that records the deed to your buyer. Ask early what that office needs, because a missing paper there can hold up the whole sale.

Get these together ahead of the closing agent's request, and check with the probate office on which ones your estate needs:

  • Certified letters proving who may sign.
  • The recorded deed or other record showing the decedent held title.
  • The newest property tax bill and payment history.
  • Names and contact details for the heirs, when there is no will.

The order of events is fairly predictable. The probate court first grants letters, and notice of appointment follows. The personal representative then collects and inventories estate property, and debts and claims are sorted out. Only then does it make sense to line up a buyer, using the powers in section 43-2-843 and the real estate rules in article 17.

At closing, taxes and any mortgage are paid, the deed goes to the judge of probate for recording with the recordation tax, and the proceeds move toward settlement and distribution under article 18. Keep each paper in one file so the title company is not chasing the estate for anything.

sections.h2: When an as-is sale suits an estate
sections.html:
An as-is sale fits when the estate has no spare time, money or energy to fix up and market the house. Probate already brings court steps, creditor questions and family choices, and a house needing a roof, a cleanout or a rehab piles on.

Cash buyers accept the house as it stands, skipping repairs, staging and showings. Authority still flows from the estate, so the personal representative works with the probate court and an Alabama attorney on timing, approvals and the deed. Heirs may weigh an offer against a regular listing and walk away owing nothing.

faqs.q: Do you always need probate to sell an inherited house in Alabama?
faqs.a: A house titled in the decedent's name generally needs someone with court-granted authority to sign, called letters testamentary or of administration, and a title company will ask to see them. Ask the county probate office whether another route fits your estate.

faqs.q: Who inherits if there is no will?
faqs.a: Under section 43-8-42, the estate goes to the decedent's issue first, then the parents, then the issue of the parents, then grandparents and their issue, after any share for a surviving spouse.

faqs.q: Can a personal representative sell real estate?
faqs.a: Yes, within the powers the will and court orders allow. Section 43-2-843 lists the transactions a representative may properly make, and article 17 of Chapter 2 deals with renting and selling real estate.

faqs.q: Are property taxes still due while the estate is open?
faqs.a: Yes. Alabama taxes are due October 1 and delinquent after December 31, and paying taxes is among the acts a personal representative may do.

faqs.q: What does it cost to record the deed, and who records it?
faqs.a: The judge of probate in the property's county records it and collects the tax, which under section 40-22-1 is 50 cents per $500 of value or fraction of $500 on conveyances above $500, plus the recording fee.
